title: Competency-Based Assessment in a Hurry: An AI-Based Alternative to Traditional Grades and the Carnegie Unit
author: Terry U
summary: A veteran assessment researcher examines the ETS-Carnegie Foundation Skills for the Future initiative, an AI-scored framework meant to measure durable skills -- collaboration, communication, and critical thinking -- as a possible successor to the century-old Carnegie credit-hour unit. He traces the partnership's timeline from its 2023 announcement through the January 2026 publication of detailed Skills Progressions, which break each skill into subskills and 31 total indicators, each rated across four developmental levels from student-submitted artifacts like group projects, presentations, and reflective journals. His central critique is that neither ETS nor Carnegie has published what evidentiary threshold in an uploaded essay or recording causes the AI to assign one developmental level over another, leaving teachers and students unable to answer why they got a given score. He grounds his skepticism historically, recalling that large-scale portfolio assessment systems in Vermont, Kentucky, and Pittsburgh in the late 1980s and early 1990s mostly failed because even trained human readers couldn't achieve acceptable interrater reliability scoring similarly holistic evidence. The piece closes as an open question about whether AI can meaningfully judge something as fluid as how well a child collaborates.
points: ETS and the Carnegie Foundation's Skills for the Future partnership is building an AI-scored, 31-indicator framework for durable skills intended to eventually replace or supplement the Carnegie credit-hour unit.

Each of the three durable skills breaks into subskills and indicators rated across four developmental levels (Exploring, Analyzing, Integrating, Extending), scored from uploaded artifacts like group projects and reflective journals.
The author's central objection is transparency: no published documentation explains what threshold of evidence in a submitted artifact causes the AI to assign one developmental level over another.

Drawing on the historical failure of large-scale portfolio assessment systems in Vermont, Kentucky, and Pittsburgh, which struggled with interrater reliability even among trained human readers, the author questions why AI scoring should be trusted as more reliable.
quotes: ETS laid off 757 California workers at the end of 2025 as its state testing contract wound down.

On April 17, 2023, the Carnegie Foundation and ETS announced a partnership to build tools for assessing "durable" skills -- collaboration, communication, and critical thinking -- that employers said matter, yet are barely legible in transcripts of course grades.

Collaboration has three subskills and seven indicators; Communication has four subskills and 15 indicators; Critical Thinking has four subskills and nine indicators -- 31 indicators in total across the three skills, each with its own four-level description

What none of these examples resolve is the question the prior section already raised: once uploaded, what threshold of evidence in an essay or a recorded discussion causes the AI to propose "Integrating" over "Analyzing" for a given indicator

If human readers -- teachers who taught writing in Vermont and Kentucky and understood the history and culture of the schools -- couldn't achieve acceptable interrater reliability for accountability purposes when assessing collections of written evidence in paper folders, on what basis would anyone be compelled to see AI scores as reliable

I am transported back in time to the era of large-scale portfolios like the system developed in Vermont in 1990 or in Kentucky in 1992 or in Pittsburgh in 1989. These systems failed for a variety of reasons, not the least of which were problems achieving reliability in scoring
